Thank you for showing me the house on a Saturday, Plácido. It’s bigger than I expected.
My pleasure, Rachel. Here is the floor plan. Three bedrooms upstairs, and the living room opens to the garden.
It looks great. Was the work done by your own team?
No, we hired a contractor. But I come every Saturday, and we had the foundation checked by an independent engineer.
That’s reassuring. What about the electrical part?
The wiring is done. This week we’re having the windows installed, and next month we’ll have the floors polished.
So when could I move in? Is the work on schedule, or did it fall behind?
Two weeks behind, because of the rain. We should hand over the keys in December, and you could still choose some of the finishes.

Look, I'll be straight with you. We're about three weeks behind. Two reasons. First, we had two weeks of heavy rain, and you can't pour concrete in that. Second, the windows were supposed to arrive on the first, and the factory delivered them on the nineteenth. We're having them installed this week. Now, I know what you're thinking: can we catch up? We can, partly. I'm bringing in two more guys for the finishes. But I'm not going to cut corners to save a week. If we rushed the plumbing and it leaked in a year, you'd never forgive me. So my honest estimate is that we hand over the keys mid-January, not the first.

My first piece of advice is: don't wait until the house is finished. As soon as the walls are up, start showing it. Buyers love to choose their own finishes, and that's a great selling point. But before the first visit, please have the site cleaned. You'd be amazed how many builders show a house full of rubbish. And have a simple floor plan printed, with the sizes of every room. Buyers want to take something home. As for the asking price, be careful. Don't set it too high at the start, hoping to negotiate. A house that sits on the market for six months looks like a problem, even if it isn't.

I always tell my clients: the last ten percent of the work is what people remember. Nobody visits a house and admires the foundation, or the plumbing inside the walls. Those are essential, of course, but they are invisible. What buyers see and touch are the finishes: the floors, the tiles, the doors, the light. That is where a good house becomes a beautiful one. In my own house in Milan, I had the old wooden floors restored instead of replacing them. It took longer and cost more, but every visitor comments on them. So my advice is: never cut corners on the structure, and never be cheap with the finishes.
